title: Handling Date and Time Variables
abstract:
Date and time columns encode seasonality, cycles and trends — and a raw
timestamp encodes none of that in a form a model can use. This document covers
the rule from the notes (never use a date directly; extract its parts, or use
sin/cos, or lags), the full catalogue of extractable features, why cyclical
encoding needs two components, the elapsed-time and lag/rolling features
that carry most of the predictive value, and the two traps that are unique to
temporal data: leakage from future information and the wrong train/test split.

blocks.t: The Rule
From the notes

items:
Date & time often encode patterns like seasonality, cycles and
 trends.

Never use a date directly. Extract date, time etc., or use
 sin/cos, lag etc.

Convert to datetime first:
 df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])

blocks.t: Why a raw timestamp is useless

A datetime stored as an integer — Unix seconds, say — is monotonically
increasing forever. A model trained on it learns "bigger number $\Rightarrow$
more sales", and every future prediction lies strictly outside the training
range. Meanwhile the actual signal — that sales rise on Fridays, peak in
December, and dip at 3 a.m. — is invisible, because none of those facts is a
monotone function of the timestamp.
What to Extract

blocks.cap:
One timestamp becomes a dozen features. Which ones matter depends
 entirely on the domain — hour is decisive for a ride-hailing model and
 irrelevant for an annual-report model.

blocks.t: Date parts

head: Feature
Accessor
Captures
rows: Continuous position in the annual cycle

blocks.t: Time parts

hour, minute, second; plus derived flags such as
is_business_hour and part_of_day. For most business problems
hour carries nearly all the intraday signal and second carries
none.
Derived features — usually the most valuable

rows: A single binary that often beats the full day-of-week one-hot
Requires a domain calendar; enormous in retail and transport
Recency; the R in RFM segmentation
The previous value, the 7-day mean, the same weekday last week

blocks.t: Elapsed time beats absolute time

days_since_signup generalises; signup_date does not. A model
trained on absolute dates has never seen 2027 and cannot reason about it, whereas
"customer is 340 days old" means the same thing in every year. Whenever
a date is meaningful only relative to something else, encode the difference, not
the date.
Cyclical Encoding with sin/cos

blocks.cap:
The problem, the fix, and why the fix needs two components. Encoded as
 an integer, hour 23 and hour 0 are 23 apart — the maximum possible distance —
 when in reality they are adjacent.

blocks.t: The encoding
For a value $v$ in a cycle of period $T$:

This maps the cycle onto the unit circle. The Euclidean distance between two
encoded points is
d = 2\left|\sin \left(\frac{\pi (v_1-v_2)}{T}\right)\right|,

which correctly returns a small value for $v_1=23,\;v_2=0$ with $T=24$, and its
maximum for values half a cycle apart.
Why two components and not one

$\sin$ alone is not injective on a full cycle: $\sin(2\pi\cdot3/24) = \sin(2\pi\cdot9/24)$, so 3 a.m. and 9 a.m. would collapse to the same value.
The pair $(\sin,\cos)$ is injective — it is the unique point on the circle.
You must always add both.
Cyclical encoding is for distance- and gradient-based models

Trees do not need it. A tree can isolate hour 23 with two splits
(hour > 22), so the wrap-around costs it almost nothing. Cyclical encoding
matters for linear models, KNN, K-Means, SVM and neural networks — anything
that treats the feature as a position on a line. For trees, one-hot or plain
integer encoding is usually as good and more interpretable.
Lag and Rolling Features

For time series, the strongest predictor of tomorrow is almost always
yesterday.

rows: The value 1 period ago, 7 periods ago (same weekday)
Change since the previous period — removes trend

blocks.t: The shift that everyone forgets

A rolling mean computed with df.rolling(7).mean() at row $t$ includes row
$t$ itself — which is the value you are trying to predict. You must
.shift(1) afterwards so the window ends at $t-1$. This is the single most
common leak in time-series feature engineering, and it produces spectacular
backtest results that vanish in production.
The Two Temporal Traps
Trap 1 — feature leakage from the future

Every feature must be computable from information available strictly
before the prediction timestamp (Topic 09). With dates this is easy to violate
accidentally: a "total spend this year" feature computed in March silently
includes April through December.
Trap 2 — the random train/test split

train_test_split(shuffle=True) on temporal data lets the model train on
March and validate on January. The score is inflated and the setup is impossible
in production. Use a chronological cut, or TimeSeriesSplit for
cross-validation, so training always precedes validation.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2026-03-01", freq="h")
df = pd.DataFrame({"ts": idx})

# a realistic signal: weekly + daily seasonality + trend + noise
t = np.arange(len(idx))
df["demand"] = (100
    + 30 * np.sin(2*np.pi*df.ts.dt.hour/24)          # daily cycle
    + 20 * (df.ts.dt.dayofweek >= 5)                 # weekend effect
    + 15 * np.sin(2*np.pi*df.ts.dt.dayofyear/365.25) # annual cycle
    + 0.002 * t                                      # trend
    + rng.normal(0, 6, len(idx)))

# =====================================================================
# 1. STEP ZERO -- convert to datetime. Nothing works before this.
# =====================================================================
df["ts"] = pd.to_datetime(df["ts"])
print(df.ts.dtype)                       # datetime64[ns]
# From a messy source you often need:
#   pd.to_datetime(s, format="%d/%m/%Y", errors="coerce", utc=True)
# `errors="coerce"` turns unparseable strings into NaT rather than crashing.

# =====================================================================
# 2. EXTRACT THE PARTS
# =====================================================================
d = df.ts.dt
feat = pd.DataFrame({
    # --- date parts ---
    "year":        d.year,
    "month":       d.month,
    "day":         d.day,
    "dayofweek":   d.dayofweek,          # Monday = 0
    "dayofyear":   d.dayofyear,
    "quarter":     d.quarter,
    "weekofyear":  d.isocalendar().week.astype(int),
    # --- time parts ---
    "hour":        d.hour,
    "minute":      d.minute,
    # --- derived flags ---
    "is_weekend":     (d.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int),
    "is_month_start": d.is_month_start.astype(int),
    "is_month_end":   d.is_month_end.astype(int),
    "is_business_hr": ((d.hour >= 9) & (d.hour < 18) & (d.dayofweek < 5)).astype(int),
})
print(feat.head(3).T)

# =====================================================================
# 3. CYCLICAL ENCODING -- both components, always
# =====================================================================
def cyclic(values, period):
    ang = 2 * np.pi * np.asarray(values) / period
    return np.sin(ang), np.cos(ang)

for name, col, period in [("hour", d.hour, 24),
                          ("dow",  d.dayofweek, 7),
                          ("month", d.month, 12),
                          ("doy",  d.dayofyear, 365.25)]:
    feat[f"{name}_sin"], feat[f"{name}_cos"] = cyclic(col, period)

# PROOF that the wrap-around is fixed:
def dist(h1, h2, period=24):
    s1, c1 = cyclic(h1, period); s2, c2 = cyclic(h2, period)
    return float(np.hypot(s1 - s2, c1 - c2))

print(f"raw integer distance 23 vs 0 : {abs(23 - 0)}")     # 23  -- WRONG
print(f"cyclic distance      23 vs 0 : {dist(23, 0):.3f}") # 0.26 -- adjacent
print(f"cyclic distance      12 vs 0 : {dist(12, 0):.3f}") # 2.00 -- maximal

# WHY BOTH COMPONENTS: sin alone is not injective
print("sin(3h) == sin(9h):", np.isclose(cyclic(3, 24)[0], cyclic(9, 24)[0]))   # True
print("(sin,cos) differ  :", not np.allclose(cyclic(3, 24), cyclic(9, 24)))    # True

# =====================================================================
# 4. ELAPSED TIME -- generalises where absolute dates do not
# =====================================================================
signup = pd.to_datetime(rng.choice(pd.date_range("2020-01-01", "2025-12-31"), 5))
now = pd.Timestamp("2026-03-01")
users = pd.DataFrame({"signup": signup})
users["days_since_signup"]  = (now - users.signup).dt.days
users["months_since_signup"] = users.days_since_signup / 30.44
users["tenure_years"]        = users.days_since_signup / 365.25
print(users)
# `days_since_signup` means the same thing in 2026 and 2030.
# `signup.year` does not -- the model has never seen 2030.

# =====================================================================
# 5. LAG AND ROLLING FEATURES -- and the shift that prevents leakage
# =====================================================================
daily = df.set_index("ts").demand.resample("D").mean().to_frame()

daily["lag_1"] = daily.demand.shift(1)          # yesterday
daily["lag_7"] = daily.demand.shift(7)          # same weekday last week

# WRONG -- the window at row t INCLUDES row t, i.e. the target itself
daily["roll7_leaky"] = daily.demand.rolling(7).mean()

# RIGHT -- shift first, so the window ends at t-1
daily["roll7"]     = daily.demand.shift(1).rolling(7).mean()
daily["roll7_std"] = daily.demand.shift(1).rolling(7).std()
daily["diff_1"]    = daily.demand.diff(1)

print(daily[["demand", "roll7_leaky", "roll7"]].head(10).round(2))
print("leaky rolling correlates with the target:",
      daily[["demand", "roll7_leaky"]].corr().iloc[0, 1].round(3))   # inflated
print("correct rolling                        :",
      daily[["demand", "roll7"]].corr().iloc[0, 1].round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 6. DOES CYCLICAL ENCODING ACTUALLY HELP? -- model-dependent
# =====================================================================
y = df.demand.values
raw_cols    = ["hour", "dayofweek", "month"]
cyclic_cols = ["hour_sin","hour_cos","dow_sin","dow_cos","month_sin","month_cos"]

tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)      # NEVER a shuffled split on time data
for model_name, model in [("Ridge (linear)", Ridge()),
                          ("RandomForest", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=60,
                                                                 random_state=0))]:
    r = cross_val_score(model, feat[raw_cols],    y, cv=tscv, scoring="r2").mean()
    c = cross_val_score(model, feat[cyclic_cols], y, cv=tscv, scoring="r2").mean()
    print(f"{model_name:16s} raw {r:6.3f}   cyclic {c:6.3f}")
# Ridge: large gain -- it cannot represent a cycle from an integer.
# Forest: little difference -- it can isolate hour 23 with two splits.

# =====================================================================
# 7. TEMPORAL SPLIT -- train on the past, validate on the future
# =====================================================================
cut = "2025-10-01"
train = df[df.ts <  cut]
test  = df[df.ts >= cut]
print(f"train {train.ts.min().date()} -> {train.ts.max().date()}  ({len(train)})")
print(f"test  {test.ts.min().date()} -> {test.ts.max().date()}  ({len(test)})")

# And what a RANDOM split would wrongly allow:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
a, b = train_test_split(df, test_size=.25, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
print("random split test range:", b.ts.min().date(), "->", b.ts.max().date())
# The "test" set spans the whole history -- the model trains on the future.

# =====================================================================
# 8. AS A PIPELINE-SAFE TRANSFORMER
# =====================================================================
def datetime_features(X):
    s = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(np.ravel(X)))
    d = s.dt
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=s.index)
    for name, col, period in [("hour", d.hour, 24), ("dow", d.dayofweek, 7),
                              ("month", d.month, 12)]:
        ang = 2 * np.pi * col / period
        out[f"{name}_sin"], out[f"{name}_cos"] = np.sin(ang), np.cos(ang)
    out["is_weekend"] = (d.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int)
    out["hour"] = d.hour
    return out.values

dt_tf = FunctionTransformer(datetime_features,
                            feature_names_out=lambda s, n: np.array(
                                ["hour_sin","hour_cos","dow_sin","dow_cos",
                                 "month_sin","month_cos","is_weekend","hour"]))

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("dt",    ColumnTransformer([("time", dt_tf, "ts")], remainder="drop")),
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", Ridge()),
])
print("pipeline r2:", cross_val_score(pipe, df[["ts"]], y, cv=tscv,
                                      scoring="r2").mean().round(3))
# Raw timestamps in, predictions out -- the extraction is part of the model.
Worked Examples
Extracting features from a date
Take the date 2026-08-30 (a Sunday).
Step 1 – calendar features.

Step 2 – why a plain month number is wrong. Month 12 and month 1 are neighbours in time, but as integers they are 11 apart. A linear or distance-based model would treat December and January as far apart.
Step 3 – cyclic encoding. Map the month onto a circle with period 12:
m_{\sin} = \sin \Big(\frac{2\pi \cdot 8}{12}\Big) = \sin(240^\circ) \approx -0.866, \qquad m_{\cos} = \cos(240^\circ) = -0.5
Distance between December $(\cos 0^\circ\!=\!1,\sin 0^\circ\!=\!0)$ and January $(\cos 30^\circ\!\approx\!0.866,\sin 30^\circ\!=\!0.5)$ is now small, as it should be.
Step 4 – parse first. The raw string must become a datetime before any of this: df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"]), then use .dt.month, .dt.dayofweek, and so on.
Summary
Everything on one page

items: Date & time encode seasonality, cycles and trends.

Never use a date directly — extract the parts, or use
 sin/cos or lags.

Extract: year, month, day, day-of-week, quarter, week-of-year,
 day-of-year, hour, minute; plus flags such as is_weekend,
 is_month_end, is_business_hour.

Elapsed time generalises; absolute dates do not. Prefer
 days_since_signup to signup_year.

Cyclical encoding:
 $\sin(2\pi v/T)$ and $\cos(2\pi v/T)$. Both components are
 required — $\sin$ alone maps two different hours to the same value.

Cyclical encoding matters for linear, distance and neural models. Trees
 do not need it.

Lag and rolling features carry most of the predictive value in
 time series — and you must .shift(1) before rolling, or you leak
 the target.

Two temporal traps: future leakage in features, and the
 random train/test split. Split chronologically; use
 TimeSeriesSplit.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why encode the hour as sin and cos rather than as an integer?

Because the hour is cyclical. As an integer, 23 and 0 are 23 apart — the maximum
possible distance — when they are actually adjacent. Mapping onto the unit
circle makes the distance correct.
Q. Why do you need both sin and cos?

$\sin$ alone is not injective over a full cycle: 3 a.m. and 9 a.m. give the same
sine. The pair identifies a unique point on the circle.
Q. Should you use cyclical encoding for XGBoost?

Rarely worth it. A tree isolates hour 23 with a couple of splits, so the
wrap-around costs it little. Cyclical encoding is for models that treat the
feature as a position on a line — linear models, KNN, SVM, neural networks.

Q. Your demand forecast has $R^2 = 0.99$ in backtest and fails live.
Most likely cause?

A rolling or aggregate feature that includes the current row — rolling(7)
without a .shift(1). The feature contains the target. Check every
window-based feature's alignment.
Q. How do you split time-series data for validation?

Chronologically: train on the past, validate on the future, mirroring production.
Use TimeSeriesSplit for cross-validation. A shuffled split lets the model
learn from the future and inflates every metric.
Q. Should you include year as a feature?

Only with care. It captures a genuine trend but cannot extrapolate — every
future year is outside the training range, and a tree will simply clamp to the
last year it saw. Prefer an explicit trend term, a time index, or elapsed-time
features.
